properties.field_incident_overview:
On May 14, 2026 a powerful storm system moved through southwest Kansas. Lightning strikes, fueled by strong winds and very dry vegetation, started multiple fires across the landscape. The fires quickly surpassed the local and mutual aid response. State assistance was requested. Aviation, KFS DFMOs, and in-state Wildfire Taskforces were mobilized. Many of the initial fires merged and are now being managed as a complex fire. Kansas Governor Kelly issued a State of Emergency Declaration on Friday, May 15, 2026. Local declarations have been issued; there is no federal emergency declaration. 

On Monday, May 18, the Meade County Fires are now under one Incident Command System and will be called the Meade Lake Complex. 

On May 20, 2026, the fire region received precipitation and higher humidity, which helped increase containment on both complexes. Non-local resources will be returned to their home units, and the fires will be monitored and patrolled by the local fire departments. The weather conditions in southwest Kansas have not dramatically changed. There is still potential for new starts to burn intensely and grow rapidly. 

The fires under the Meade Lake Complex are the Wolf Canyon Fire, the Meade County Complex 1 and 2, the Proffitt Lake fire, and the 2 unstaffed fires in the southern part of the county.  

Meade Lake Complex -  Jeff Latham and Troy Mueller - Incident Commanders      

  • 91,616 acres
  • 100% contained

The 500-Acre Pond Fire and the Herman Range Fire grew together on Sunday May, 17, 2026. All fires in Clark County will also be a complex of fires. The complex will include the Bouziden Range Fire and the Lexington Fire

Herman Range Complex - Chad Maybery Incident Commander

On Monday, May 18, 2026, the Herman Ranch Fire made a significant run to the south when the forecasted cold front impacted the fire’s open containment lines along the southern edge of the incident. The acres and map do not reflect that event.

  • 90% Contained

properties.field_incident_overview:
The South Fork Fire ignited on June 9, 2026, in the Soldier Creek Wilderness area of the Nebraska National Forest’s Pine Ridge Ranger District near Crawford, Nebraska. Local responders, U.S. Forest Service crews and volunteer firefighting partners engaged the fire early as dry fuels, steep terrain and strong winds drove rapid spread. U.S. Highway 20 was closed by the Nebraska Department of Transportation as the fire jumped the highway. A red flag warning was in effect through Wednesday, June 10.

By June 10, the fire had grown to nearly 9,000 acres and Nebraska’s Governor Pillen officially issued an emergency declaration for the South Fork Fire. It was fueled by rugged terrain, dry vegetation including timber and grassy undergrowth, and strong winds. On June 11 at 6 am the Rocky Mountain Complex Incident Management Team 2, under the command of Jay Mickey, assumed control of the fire.

On June 12, containment increased to 7% even as the fire grew to about 28,067 acres. Resources including National Guard units, ground crews, dozers and aircraft focused on defending the towns of Crawford and the Fort Robinson State Park area. The Red Cross established community shelter options at the Chadron State College–Andrews Hall.

By June 15, containment was at 55% and the fire had grown to 38,914 acres. 581 personnel were supporting the fire. Forecasters predicted that the week ahead would bring sustained winds anticipated between 23 and 30 miles per hour, and the possibility of gusts escalating to as high as 50 miles per hour. 

Nebraska’s Governor, Jim Pillen received an operational visit of the South Fork Fire on June 16. He visited ICP and was provided with a comprehensive briefing. He had the opportunity to communicate with members of his constituency as well as incident team members. 

Containment reached 80% on June 17, with the acres climbing to 39,057. Although conditions continued to change, fire activity was generally quiet. A NIROPS flight (a thermal imaging aircraft used to map active wildfires) was ordered after several areas of hot spots were discovered. 

Line is now in place around the entire fire perimeter. Crews are working to secure and mop up the containment line and will continue for several days. Suppression repair work is also u begin underway and will continue in the next few days. 

On June 20th the overall acreage of the South Fork Fire increased to 39,696 due to more accurate satellite mapping showing previously unseen grassy areas and containment increased to 90%.

Rocky Mountain CIMT2 transfered command to the Nebraska Type 3 team on Sunday, June 21, 2026, at 6 p.m.  

Please follow the Nebraska National Forest on Facebook and the Nebraska National Forest website's Alerts and Notices page for further updates.

The Flat Fire is a lightning-caused wildfire located approximately 9 miles southwest of Heber, Arizona within Navajo Count. The fire is currently estimated at 134 acres and is 83% contained. The incident will transition on June 29th at 6:00am from the White Mountain Zone Type 3 team to a Type 4 organization.

During the current operational period, fire activity remained minimal, consisting primarily of smoldering and creeping within the interior. Firefighters will continue mop up operations and perimeter patrols to secure containment lines and keep the fire within the established perimeter. Fuels consist primarily of medium logging slash, brush, and tall grasses.

A Red Flag Warning remains in effect through Sunday evening, with dry breezy conditions and near-critical fire weather expected to continue into next week. Gusty winds may produce interior flare ups and localized spotting potential over the next 72 hours; however, no current threat to communities, infrastructure, or other values at risk has been identified.

There has been no reported damage to structures or infrastructure, no civilian impacts. Approximately 192 personnel remain assigned to the incident in support of suppression and containment efforts.

Operational priorities remained focused on patrolling and securing the fire perimeter, completing mop-up where needed, implementing suppression repair, and maintaining containment.

Fire managers are implementing direct extinguishment and indirect confinement strategies on the Kinky Creek Fire. A direct extinguishment strategy is when firefighters engage the active flame front directly to stop fire spread. An indirect confinement strategy is when firefighters work away from the active flame front to steer or contain the fire.

The forest has issued a trail closure order.

The fire danger rating is currently “high” for the Teton Interagency Dispatch area, which includes Bridger-Teton National Forest, Grand Teton National Park, and the National Elk Refuge.

properties.field_incident_overview:
Situation: The lightning-caused Mt. Tom Creek Fire is burning high on a remote mountain slope on the west side of Olympic National Park. The area is in steep, densely forested terrain approximately five miles west‑northwest of Mount Olympus. Backpackers first reported the fire on June 24th.

The fire is approximately six miles from the Hoh Rain Forest administrative site. The Hoh Rain Forest Visitor Center, campground, and trails all remain open to the public.

Firefighters are using indirect confinement tactics as part of a full-suppression strategy. These tactics include removing vegetation around recreation and administrative infrastructure and using helicopters to drop water to cool host spots and keep the fire within its current footprint. The fire is constrained by natural features on a couple flanks, where fire managers have determined it is 27% contained.

High relative humidity and periodic precipitation may constrain fire behavior, but are unlikely to extinguish the fire.

Smoke: Smoke may be visible from various locations on the Olympic Peninsula. Air quality can change quickly.  For current smoke information, visit: https://fire.airnow.gov

Fire Restrictions: Olympic National Park implemented fire restrictions June 25th. Dispersed and backcountry fires are prohibited. Fires within established metal fire rings in developed campgrounds and picnic areas are exempt from this prohibition. Propane and gas stoves are allowed, if operated at least three feet away from flammable vegetation and forest litter.

Air Space Restrictions: A Temporary Flight Restriction is in place. If you fly, we can’t. Every time a drone is spotted near the fire all aircraft are grounded until we can be sure the drone is clear of this area: http://knowbeforeyoufly.org

The Wild Goose Fire began on June 26, 2026 just south of Wild Goose Canyon on the Fishlake National Forest. It is located east of Holden and south of Scipio, Utah. The fire burned in mixed fuel types and steep terrain. The fire grew very quickly in the first 24 hours, prompting evacuations of nearby communities and a closure order on Fishlake National Forest.

In the first days of the incident, cooler temperatures allowed firefighters to actively engage the fire, installing containment and contingency lines before increased temperatures and heavier winds created critical fire weather conditions. 

Fuels are exceptionally dry for this time of year and contributed to extreme fire behavior, but the lines created in the first week of GBT7's tenure have held and largely curtailed fire spread. Since July 3, fire behavior has remained moderate. On July 10, all evacuation orders were lifted and the Fishlake National Forest Closure was reduced in size to reopen popular recreation areas to the south of the fire.

On July 11 at 1900, command of the fire transitioned back to a local Type 4 Incident Commander on the Fishlake National Forest.

The fire is located approximately 15 miles northwest of Dolores, Colorado on the San Juan National Forest, Bureau of Land Management, and private lands.

Strong winds, high heat, low humidity and extremely dry fuels drove fire behavior for the first two weeks before monsoonal moisture moved into Southwest Colorado. More favorable weather beginning in mid July, including several days of rain, cloud coverage, and higher humidity levels, helped firefighters increase containment and stop fire progression. Now, as the fire nears containment, crews are working on suppression repair to leave the area in the best condition possible. This work involves repairing roads, naturalizing dozer line, chipping cut brush and trees, clearing culverts, and removing hose, pumps, and other equipment.

Evacuations and Closures:  All evacuations have been lifted. You can follow Dolores County Office of Emergency Management and/or San Miguel County Sheriff for those respective counties' emergency notifications. The Gold Mountain Fire was discovered on June 27, 2026, at approximately 5:33 pm 2 miles northeast of Ouray, CO. Fire initially started burning in mixed conifer vegetation located on inaccessible terrain above the east side of Highway 550. Local, State, and Federal initial attack fire resources were ordered immediately. The fire spread quickly running up steep slopes. A local Type 3 Incident Management Team was assigned on June 27, 2026. Aviation resources were ordered throughout the next day, but high winds and terrain features shut down the use of aviation resources. Fire became very active, with group torching and crowning, increasing the fire growth to the east by 2,000 acres. Fire resources provided public safety and worked to protect structures. Rocky Mountain Complex Incident Management Team 3 was ordered on June 28, 2026, and took command on June 29, 2026, at 6 pm.  Red Flag conditions over the following week led to extreme fire behavior increasing the fire growth to over 30,000 acres by July 6, 2026.  Rocky Mountain Complex Incident Management Team 2 assumed command July 14, 2026 following a coordinated, planned transition.  Rocky Mountain Complex Incident Management Team 1 assumed command July 26, 2026 following a coordinated, planned transition. 

Firefighters are using a risk-based suppression strategy that prioritizes public and firefighter safety while protecting communities, critical infrastructure, water systems and access along the Highway 550 corridor. Crews continue to mop up and strengthen fire lines near Highway 550 and Cow Creek, secure the fire edge around Nate Creek, and construct and reinforce indirect line along the western perimeter toward Bureau of Land Management lands and south toward Silver Jack Reservoir. 

Where direct engagement is unsafe or impractical, firefighters are using natural features, indirect containment lines, point protection around homes and other values at risk, and pumps, hoses and large water tanks to support structure protection. Aerial resources continue to monitor and support operations along inaccessible portions of the fire. Although thunderstorms may bring periods of rain, critically dry fuels, lightning and erratic outflow winds remain concerns.
properties.title: Gold Mountain Fire

properties.field_incident_overview:
Background: On the afternoon of Sunday, June 21, the Mogollon Baldy lookout detected a lightning-caused fire on Sacaton Mountain (elevation 10,658 feet) in the Gila Wilderness. The fire, which is on the Glenwood Ranger District, was initially about 4.5 miles west of the lookout tower. 

Firefighters quickly conducted an aerial assessment and estimated the fire—burning in brush, timber, logs, and snags—was about 2 acres and exhibiting moderate fire behavior. By late evening, the lookout reported the fire had grown to approximately 4 acres.

The fire’s location presents extreme risks to both ground and aerial firefighters: It is burning among numerous snags, a dense tangle of fallen trees, and thick brush regeneration from the 2012 Whitewater-Baldy Fire. The landscape is very rugged and steep (e.g., 40–60 percent slopes). Safety zones and escape routes are nonexistent. Emergency extraction times would be unacceptably long (i.e., 6+ hours) and logistically difficult. High-elevation flying, especially during hot weather, is very hazardous and an unacceptable transfer of risk to the pilot.

Smoke & Air Quality: Smoke is visible from numerous areas in and surrounding the Gila National Forest. Scroll down for air quality information and the AirNow Fire and Smoke Map.

properties.field_incident_description:
Recent rainfall and reduced fire activities is allowing firefighters to engage fires across the area more directly, digging containment lines and laying hoses more closely to the fires’ edges where possible.
Non-Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness Wildfires
• Camp: 4,397 acres; 46% contained. Location – 5 miles north of Winton. Crews patrolled and extinguished hot spots deeper into the fire’s southern and western perimeters and assessed structures on the Cloquet Line. Crews were flown into the northeast section of the fire to scout and plan for opportunities to construct fireline and lay hose closer to the fire’s edge.
• Sioux: 12,576 acres; 27% contained. Location – North of the Echo Trail and east of Jeanette Campground. Portions of the fire are burning in BWCAW. Crews continued patrolling and extinguishing hot spots in the portion of the fire that burned south of Echo Trail. Crews are also preparing to lay hose more directly along the fire’s southeast perimeter north of Echo Trail. Structure protection continues in the Moose Loop and Meander Lake areas.
Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness Wildfires
• Little Knife: 4,958 acres; 49% contained. Originated in Ontario and crossed into the United States on July 15. Wildland firefighters are working to secure peninsulas along the southwest side of the fire. Firefighters on the northeast side of the fire are using natural features such as lakes and streams, as well as improving portage trails, for indirect containment lines. Crews continue structure protection and assessments in the Gunflint Trail corridor. No significant fire behavior is expected today; however, heat remains in the duff beneath the surface. A community meeting is planned for 7 p.m. July 29 at the Gunflint Volunteer Fire Department Fire Hall 1. The Little Knife Fire is being managed by the National Incident Management Organization.



• Bear Trap (Bear Trap and Dark Fires combined): 37,837 total acres (29,767 acres in the United States); 38% contained. Location – South of Lac La Croix, 20 miles north of Ely. Crews are widening the fuel break along Echo Trail to at least 100 feet as a contingency if the fire makes a southernly run. Crews also made progress laying hose close to the fire’s south and southeast perimeters. Chipping continues around structures at Big Lake and along Echo Trail, and hand crews are removing brush along the Angleworm Trail. A drone is also deployed over the area conducting infrared reconnaissance for heat sources.
• Thumb: 17,236 total acres (16,890 acres in the United States); 56% contained. Remote and located 6 miles south of Gakijiwanong Anishnaabe Nation Canada. The fire has been exhibiting minimal growth and activity and is being monitored by aircraft.
Wildfires West of Echo Lake and East of U.S. Hwy 53
• Chub:  424 acres. 95% contained. Location – North of Chub Lake, southwest of Crane Lake. Crews are patrolling the perimeter and extinguishing residual pockets of heat. 
• 493, Echo 2, Beaver Tail, Ridge, Creek, Marion Creek Trail, Nine, Camp 5/Duck, Bug Creek, Coffin Fires: 64.4 acres combined for all 10 fires. All are 100% contained. Crews continue to patrol these fires, searching for smoke and hot spots and extinguishing any lingering heat.
• Long Lake Fire: 15 acres. Crews are patrolling the perimeter and extinguishing residual pockets of heat.

A lightning storm moved through the Tri-Forest area on the evening of July 7, 2026, igniting multiple fires. The Salmon Fire was discovered shortly after midnight, and the Olive Butte Fire was discovered that morning on July 8, 2026. Initial attack resources responded promptly but were spread thin due to a number of other starts in the area. NW Team 12 took command of the Salmon and Olive Butte fires along with five smaller fires on July 11 at 6 AM. The five small fires were contained by the evening of July 11, but two larger fires remain burning in very steep terrain with heavy dead and downed trees that are drier than normal for this time of year and readily consuming. This heavy fuel loading also has slowed line construction efforts, coupled with running fire and long-range spotting creating a very dynamic and rapidly changing fire environment.

Evacuation notices for the communities of Greenhorn, Olive Creek, and Granite of Baker and Grant Counties are in effect. From July 12-17, the Oregon State Fire Marshal’s Green Incident Management Team, along with four structural task forces, supported structure protection operations.

Priorities remain public and firefighter safety, homes and cabins, private lands, and critical infrastructure. Firefighters are working the fires as directly as possible to protect these values at risk, using both ground resources and multiple helicopters and fixed wing aircraft dropping water and retardant.

The fire has also spread into the North Fork John Day Wilderness with additional natural resource values at risk.

The Biscar Fire started from a lightning strike on July 18, 2026 within Lassen County.  It grew quickly with warm temperatures and strong winds pushing it eastward across Highway 395.  It is currently mapped at 69,352 acres with 97% containment.

Fire Activity: Fire activity has been minimal despite elevated fire weather conditions. Containment lines around the fire continue to be reinforced. Crews have been checking integrity of the containment lines using a tactic called “cold trailing,” where fire fighters walk along these lines to verify that no heat persists. 

About 200 firefighters were released Sunday, and additional 200 were released Monday and made available to other fires in the region.  Resources continue to be made available for reassignments today as they finish their tasks on the Biscar Fire.  A National Preparedness Level 5 (Highest Level) indicates a significant amount of fire activity nationally with resources (crews, engines, aircraft) mostly being committed; and therefore fewer resources available to respond to new ignitions.

California Interagency Incident Management Team 3 has demobilized from the Biscar Fire today, and will be reassigned to the Castle Fire in southern Oregon.  The Team thanks the residents and Emergency Management staff of Lassen County, CA and Washoe County, NV for their support and dedication during the Biscar Fire.

Why the strange name?  Fires are often named after geographic features near the fire, and in this case, Biscar Reservoir is located just a few miles south of where the fire was first reported.  Pierre “Pete” Biscar (1881–1947),  was a French-born rancher who settled in Secret Valley, California, and constructed the first reservoir at the mouth of Snowstorm Canyon.

Incident Objectives:

  • Provide safety for first responders and the public through risk analysis and hazard mitigation.
  • Minimize acres burned utilizing direct extinguishment tactics.
  • Utilize resources where they can be most successful and ensure tactics have a high probability of success.
  • Protect and minimize impacts to communities, private property, infrastructure, cultural, natural resources and Sage Grouse habitat.

The Shingle Fire started  during widespread lightning event on July 23, 2026.  Located 14 Miles SE of Mitchell, Oregon.  It is currently estimated at 63,253 acres, and is 6% contained.

Current Situation: Great Basin Complex Incident Management Team 5, under Incident Commander Trent Ingram, assumed command of the Shingle Fire this morning. They are operating in Unified Command with the Oregon State Fire Marshal, Incident Commander Steve Bregman.

Yesterday, firefighters established two dozer lines surrounding the town of Dayville. Hotshots prepped along these lines by removing vegetation to reinforce containment. On the north and northwest fire flanks, crews worked to prevent forward progress near Highway 26, while strengthening existing containment lines. Crews completed strategic firing operations along Forest Road 12 on the southern and western perimeter of the fire, creating an anchor point on the west side that connects to Highway 26. These actions increased containment in the northwestern fire edge.

A third structural task force from the Oregon State Fire Marshal arrived and will deploy to the Highway 26 corridor. Other task forces continue to defend threatened structures in Antone Ranch and in the Cottonwood and Rattlesnake Road areas. These crews are completing structural preparation work to enhance defensibility in case the fire reaches those areas.

July 27, 2026, noon update on North Fork Fire

A reconnaissance flight was performed today over the North Fork Lost Horse Fire showing minimal fire growth. 

Multiple resources are here, such as heavy equipment, water tenders, fire engines and hand crews who will be working on creating fuel breaks and preventing fire growth south of Lost Horse Road and north and west of Coyote Coulee Road. The fire's perimeter was mapped at 105 acres July 26 which included outlying hotspots. 

Lost Horse Road is closed at the Lick Creek Road (Forest Service Road 5621) junction for resources responding to the fire and for public safety. A closure is also in place near the Coyote Coulee trailhead. Signs and road guards will be in place. 

The North Fork Lost Horse Fire started July 24, 2026 at 8:26 p.m. caused by a lightning strike after several thunderstorm cells passed through the area. This fire is in steep, rocky terrain on the top 1/3 of an 8,000-foot slope.

Fire activity increased July 25 due to extreme heat, low relative humidities and wind gusts exceeding 40 mph along. Three helicopters performed bucket drops throughout the day to reduce the fire's spread. Fire activity held at 40 acres on the North Fork Lost Horse Fire during evening hours of July 25 and into the morning of July 26. Decreased winds, lower temperatures and higher relative humidities helped keep the fire at bay. There was little fire activity at the top of the ridge but there was some roll out down the canyon with the fire flanking east.

Current Situation: On Monday, California Interagency Incident Management Team 5 arrived in Vale, Oregon, to take command of the ongoing Hat Fire. We want to take a moment to acknowledge and commend the dedicated firefighters who have been working around the clock, facing challenging conditions to contain and suppress the Hat Fire. Through their efforts, significant progress has been made to successfully hold the fire in its current footprint, with no new growth yesterday.   

Today, firefighters will continue to monitor and secure the area while improving the existing containment lines. Additional firefighters have arrived to assist in constructing a hand line in areas where dozers cannot be effectively used. They will also focus on mopping up along the fire’s edge and extinguishing any burning or smoldering vegetation. This process may take several days to ensure that there is no threat to the containment lines. 

Weather and Air Quality: The large high-pressure dome anchored over the Desert Southwest will continue through late week, bringing warm temperatures and low relative humidity. Wildfire smoke from fires across Oregon and southwest Idaho will cause persistent haze and degraded air quality. 

Cooperating Agencies: Juntura RFPA

properties.field_incident_description:
The Big Grass Fire started on July 23, 2026, following a lightning strike. Fuels in the area consist of brush, short grasses, and tall grasses. The fire will continue to exhibit extreme fire behavior, with rapid rates of spread in all directions when smoke lifts and winds pick up in the afternoon.

The fire has advanced to the point where protection of the wildland-urban interface has become the primary operational focus. Point protection operations are underway for multiple residences as the fire continues to progress. Continued fire spread is expected into Idaho along both the northern and southern portions of the fire area, with steady eastward progression up South Mountain.

Numerous residential structures, outbuildings, and associated improvements remain threatened as the fire continues to advance toward the community of Jordan Valley. Additional values at risk include the Wild and Scenic River corridor, North Fork Campground, Three Forks Campground, priority sage-grouse habitat, essential pronghorn habitat, grazing allotments, a Remote Automated Weather Station (RAWS), the South Mountain communication site, and numerous mining operations farther north. Continued fire spread has the potential to impact residential properties, critical infrastructure, recreational facilities, wildlife habitat, rangeland resources, and fire weather monitoring capabilities.
properties.field_incident_overview:
Current Situation: On Monday, California Interagency Incident Management Team 5 arrived in Vale, Oregon, to take command of the ongoing Big Grass Fire. We want to take a moment to acknowledge and commend all of the firefighters and the emergency personnel who have been working in challenging conditions to suppress the Big Grass Fire.  

Yesterday, the fire, which is burning in brush and grass, exhibited extreme behavior with rapid rates of spread, particularly in the afternoon when the winds picked up. Suppression efforts will remain focused on limiting fire growth while protecting threatened communities, residences, livestock, and critical infrastructure.  

Today, crews will continue to identify and establish effective anchor points to secure containment lines ahead of the advancing fire. The priority areas are in the northeast near Jordan Creek, focusing on reducing the threat to Silver City, and in the southeast near the North Fork of the Owyhee River. 

Weather and Air Quality: The large high-pressure dome anchored over the Desert Southwest will continue through late week, bringing warm temperatures and low relative humidity. Wildfire smoke from fires across Oregon and southwest Idaho will cause persistent haze and degraded air quality. 

Area Closure:   

Access to the North Fork Campground along Juniper Mountain Road in Owyhee County is temporarily closed. This closure is necessary to ensure the safety of both the public and firefighters involved in suppression efforts. 

Cooperating Agencies: Jordan Valley RFPA, Owyhee RFPA, Malheur County Sheriff’s Office, Owyhee County Sheriff’s Office.

properties.field_incident_description:
The fire remains active in grass, brush and timber. Warm, dry, and breezy weather, combined with steep terrain, has
contributed to active fire behavior, including uphill runs and spot fires. Similar weather conditions are expected to
continue through the middle of the week. Smoke from nearby wildfires may also reduce visibility and influence
local weather conditions.
properties.field_incident_overview:
The Tartar Fire, located approximately 21 miles northwest of Weiser, Idaho, was reported on July 24. The lightning-caused fire is burning in grass, brush and timber across a combination of private, Bureau of Land Management, US Forest Service, and State of Idaho lands.

Great Basin Complex Incident Management Team 3 assumed command of the fire on Tuesday, July 28. Due to recent significant fire runs and anticipated growth to the north-northwest, residents and visitors should be aware of changes to public access. Visit these sites for current closure information:

  • Payette National Forest Alerts page- https://www.fs.usda.gov/r04/payette/alerts
  • BLM-managed lands in Idaho, Public Input and Actions Page - https://www.blm.gov/public-input-actions?region[]=22
